subject: political-science
lectureTitle: EU II: Institutions of the EU (AUW)
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: Bulmer, Parker, Bache, George & Burns (2020), Politics in the EU, 5th ed. — ch. 12, "The Institutional Architecture" (pp. 205–237)

cards.front: Where does EU authority sit? Name the **three ways** authority is distributed and the **two levels** it runs across — and the umbrella term for the whole design.
cards.back:
There is **no single sovereign** in the EU. Authority to *propose, decide, implement & enforce* is distributed in **three ways**:

**① Pooled** (states decide together) · **② Delegated** (handed to a common body) · **③ Shared**.

**Two levels:** the **EU level** (European Council · Commission · Council · Parliament · CJEU) and the **member-state level** (national governments · legislatures · administrations · courts).

The umbrella term: **multi-level governance** — the same task is split between European *and* national bodies.
cards.hint: Pooled/delegated/shared, across two levels.

cards.front: Since Lisbon the EU has **no constitution but two treaties.** Which treaty sets out: (a) broad principles, the general role of institutions, **Art. 50** (leaving) and **CFSP** — and which sets out the detailed operation and all other policy areas (the **"Union method"**)?
cards.back:
(a) The **TEU** (Treaty on European Union) — broad principles, institutions' general role, accession/exit (**Art. 50**, new in Lisbon) and **CFSP** (kept largely outside the Court).

(b) The **TFEU** (Treaty on the Functioning of the EU) — detailed operation + all other policy areas, run by the **"Union method"** (Bulmer's updated name for the old "Community method").

**Lisbon (in force Dec 2009)** abolished the old **three-pillar structure** and merged everything except **CFSP** into one order. Every EU act must cite its **treaty base** — so *which article* is chosen decides the procedure.
cards.hint: Two treaties; one keeps CFSP and Art. 50.

cards.front: The backbone table: name the **five EU bodies**, whose interest each represents, and split them into **supranational vs intergovernmental**.
cards.back:
**European Council** — heads of state/government → **national governments**; sets strategic direction (not a legislator).
**Council of the EU** — national ministers → **member-state governments**; co-legislates.
**European Parliament** — elected MEPs → **EU citizens**; co-legislates + oversight.
**European Commission** — Commissioners + civil service → the **Union-wide interest**; proposes, implements, enforces.
**CJEU** — judges → the **EU legal order**; interprets & adjudicates.

**Supranational** (serve the Union, above states): **Commission · EP · CJEU**.
**Intergovernmental** (they *are* the states): **European Council · Council**.

Every EU decision is a negotiation between these two logics — *this split is the red thread of the lecture.*
cards.hint: Each body = a different constituency; then sort supra vs inter.

cards.front: **Summit of the 27 heads of state/government (+ its President + the Commission President). Sets broad priorities and unblocks the biggest fights — but does NOT legislate.** Which body? And why is it the intergovernmental heart?
cards.back:
The **European Council** — the EU's **political compass**, not its legislature. It defines **broad political priorities**, provides **strategic direction**, resolves major disputes ministers can't, and gives "**political impetus**."

It's the **intergovernmental heart** because it *is literally the national governments in the room* — in an **LI** reading, where the "masters of the treaty" steer.

*Don't confuse it with the Council of the EU (ministers) or the Council of Europe (a separate non-EU human-rights body).*
cards.hint: Leaders' summit; direction, not law.

cards.front: **Holds the right of initiative — proposes almost all EU law — then implements it and polices compliance; represents the Union-wide interest.** Which body, and what are its **four jobs**?
cards.back:
The **European Commission** — the EU's **executive and motor**.

**Four jobs (PROPOSE · EXECUTE · ENFORCE · REPRESENT):**
**① Proposes** — the **right of initiative** (sets the agenda).
**② Executes** — manages EU programmes & funding.
**③ Enforces** — as **Guardian of the Treaties**, launches **infringement proceedings** (Art. 258 TFEU).
**④ Represents** — speaks for the EU internationally where it has competence (e.g. trade).

In a **neofunctionalist** reading it's the **"cultivated spillover"** actor — the Eurocrat pushing integration forward.
cards.hint: Right of initiative; the engine.

cards.front: "The Commission proposes" — but the **right of initiative is contested, not absolute** *(Bulmer)*. Name the **five ways** the monopoly is hedged.
cards.back:
The Commission is *formally* the sole initiator, but it's boxed in:

**① European Council** sets the strategic agenda it then follows.
**② EP can request a proposal** (Art. 225 TFEU) — hard to ignore.
**③ Council can too** (Art. 241).
**④ A Conciliation Committee** can agree a text the Commission didn't write.
**⑤** It always **consults widely** (interest groups, national experts) first.

→ So "Commission proposes" is real but **shared** — an inter-institutional negotiation, not a dictate.
cards.hint: European Council · EP · Council · conciliation · consultation.

cards.front: **National ministers who change membership by topic (ECOFIN, Agriculture…); co-legislates with the EP; chaired by a presidency that rotates every 6 months in "trios."** Which body — and where does the real bargaining happen?
cards.back:
The **Council of the EU** ("the Council") — member states as legislators. It meets in **configurations by policy area** (ministers show up per dossier) and decides usually by **QMV**.

**The presidency rotates every 6 months in "trios"** of three states planning an 18-month agenda — a relay baton, not a throne.

**Most work happens *below* the ministers:** national ministers ← **COREPER I & II** (permanent reps/ambassadors) ← **working parties + national officials** ← Council Secretariat. "Much of the bargaining happens among diplomats *before* ministers meet." *(The "bureaucratic interpenetration" neofunctionalism talks about.)*

Despite QMV, ministers usually decide by **consensus** (Häge 2013).
cards.hint: Ministers, trios, COREPER.

cards.front: **The EU's only directly elected body — members grouped by transnational political family, not by nation; once a "talking shop," now co-legislates as an equal.** Which body, and how is it organised?
cards.back:
The **European Parliament (EP)** — the citizens' chamber.

**Who:** **MEPs, directly elected every 5 years**, sitting in cross-national **political groups** (a group needs ≥ **23 MEPs from ≥ 7 states**), seated left-to-right by **ideology**.

**What it does:** **co-legislates** with the Council under the **OLP**; can **amend or block**; **oversees** the Commission (approves and can **censure** it).

It gained real power through successive treaties — its co-equal status is a major **deepening** of supranational democracy. *(After 2024: EPP largest, then S&D; centre holds a working majority.)*
cards.hint: Elected; political families, not countries.

cards.front: **The EU's supreme court: interprets the treaties, ensures the law means the same thing everywhere, draws the boundary between EU and national authority — and can push integration forward with no new treaty.** Which body?
cards.back:
The **Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU)**.

It **interprets** the treaties & legislation, ensures **uniform application**, resolves disputes, and **draws the EU/national boundary**.

Key integration point: "**courts can shape integration**" — by deciding what EU law requires, it advances **"integration through law"** without any new treaty (the neofunctionalist channel; see *Cassis*).

*Not to be confused with the European Court of Human Rights (Council of Europe).*
cards.hint: The court; "integration through law."

cards.front: Beyond the five, two **advisory bodies** have a right to be *consulted* *(Bulmer)*. Distinguish the **EESC** from the **Committee of the Regions (CoR)** — and say which is more influential and why.
cards.back:
**EESC (European Economic & Social Committee)** — reps of **employers, workers & "various interests"** (farmers, consumers, professions); **329 members** in a personal capacity. Consulted on social/single-market policy — but **not very influential, overshadowed by the elected EP**.

**CoR (Committee of the Regions)** — reps of **regional & local government**, created by **Maastricht (1994)**. *More* influential because **backed by powerful actors** — pushed by the **German Länder** fearing loss of *their* powers to Brussels.

The CoR made itself champion of **"multi-level governance"** and a natural **ally of the Commission** against central governments — a **subnational echo of cultivated spillover**.
cards.hint: Civil society vs regions; the Länder's baby.

cards.front: **The EU's financial watchdog — created 1975, based in Luxembourg, one member per state; checks revenue and spending are lawful, publishes an annual report that grounds the EP's budget sign-off.** Which body? *(Bulmer)*
cards.back:
The **European Court of Auditors** — **audits EU finances**.

Created **1975**, in **Luxembourg**; **one member per state** (6-yr renewable term), ~850 staff (two-thirds auditors). It checks revenue and spending were **lawful and regular** and publishes an **annual report** — the basis for the EP's **budget discharge**.
cards.hint: Auditors; feeds the EP's discharge.

cards.front: The EU has **no general power to act** — only conferred **competences**, in three strengths. Distinguish **exclusive · shared · supporting** (with examples). What **fourth head** does Bulmer add?
cards.back:
**Exclusive** — **only the EU** may legislate: customs union, single currency, competition rules, common commercial (trade) policy, fisheries conservation.
**Shared** — **EU *and* states** (states act where the EU hasn't): internal market, environment, transport, consumer protection.
**Supporting** — **states legislate; EU only supports/coordinates**: culture, education, tourism *(health systems, taxation, defence stay largely national)*.

**Bulmer's fourth head** *(Insight 12.1, Arts. 3–6 TFEU):* a distinct **"policy co-ordination"** category for members' **economic, employment & social** policies (EU coordinates, doesn't legislate). *(CFSP sits outside this TFEU catalogue — it's in the TEU.)* Lisbon spelt the catalogue out for the first time — a **German-Länder demand** to stop competence drifting upward.
cards.hint: EU-only / both / states-lead — plus policy co-ordination.

cards.front: Name and define the **three constitutional principles** that fence in EU power.
cards.back:
**① Conferral** — the EU may act **only where the treaties give it competence**. No treaty basis → no EU action. *(Default: power stays national.)*
**② Subsidiarity** — in **non-exclusive** areas, the EU should act **only when the objective can't be adequately achieved by member states** alone (decisions as close to citizens as effective).
**③ Proportionality** — EU action must **not go beyond what is necessary** to achieve its aim (use the lightest tool that works).
cards.hint: Only-if-conferred · only-if-better-at-EU-level · no-more-than-necessary.

cards.front: Run the **Ordinary Legislative Procedure (OLP / co-decision)** — the "typical" way an EU law is made — step by step. What is its defining feature?
cards.back:
**① Commission** — agenda-sets and **proposes** (right of initiative).
**② EP + Council** — each examines and **amends** the proposal.
**③ Negotiation / readings** — the two co-legislators reconcile versions (often **trilogue** with the Commission).
**④ Agreement** — **both** EP **and** Council approve the **same text**.
**⑤ Adopted → implemented & enforced.**

**Defining feature:** **Parliament and Council co-decide as equals** — the citizens' chamber and the states' chamber must *both* say yes; either can **amend or block**. This co-equal status is a major deepening won over successive treaties (from Maastricht's codecision onward).
cards.hint: Commission proposes; EP + Council both must agree.

cards.front: How does the Council decide by **Qualified Majority Voting (QMV)**? Give the **double threshold**, why there are two locks, and the radical implication.
cards.back:
A proposal passes with a **double majority**:
**① 55% of member states** (≥ **15 of 27**), **AND**
**② states representing 65% of the EU population.**

**Two locks:** the **55%** protects the **many small** states (one state, one vote); the **65% population** protects the **few large** ones. Both majorities are needed. *(A blocking minority needs ≥ 4 states — so no 3 big states can veto alone.)*

**Radical implication:** a national government can be **outvoted and still bound** — the sharpest evidence the EU is more than an ordinary IO.

*(Bulmer:* if the proposal is **not** from the Commission the bar rises to **72% of states**. QMV is now the **default** — Art. 16(3) TEU — after a long march from the **SEA 1986**. **Unanimity** still rules the sensitive areas: foreign/security policy, taxation, social security, defence, enlargement, language, seat of institutions.)*
cards.hint: 55% states + 65% population; you can lose.

cards.front: Lisbon made the **OLP the default**, but two **"special legislative procedures"** survive where states kept more control *(Bulmer)*. Distinguish **consultation** from **consent** — how strong is the EP in each?
cards.back:
**Consultation** — the Commission proposes; the **Council must *ask* the EP's opinion but can then ignore it**, and decides (often by **unanimity**). The **CJEU's *Isoglucose* ruling (1980)** at least forces the Council to *wait for* the opinion. Now ~20 areas only.

**Consent** (ex-"assent") — the EP **cannot amend**, but its **yes is required** — a **veto**. Main use: **international agreements**, including **accession** of new members, and the multi-annual budget framework.

→ EP is **weakest** under consultation (opinion, ignorable), holds a **blunt veto** under consent, and is **co-equal** only under the OLP.
cards.hint: Ignorable opinion vs a yes/no veto.

cards.front: Lisbon let **national parliaments police subsidiarity** via "cards" *(Bulmer)*. Explain the **yellow** and **orange** cards — thresholds, effect, and use.
cards.back:
**Yellow card:** if ~**one-third** of national parliaments, within **8 weeks**, issue a **reasoned opinion** that a proposal breaches **subsidiarity**, the Commission must **review** it (maintain, amend, or withdraw).

**Orange card:** stronger — a **simple majority** of parliaments that, if backed by Council or EP, can **kill** the proposal. **Never used.**

**Yellow card played 3 times:** **2012 "right-to-strike" (Monti II)** → Commission **withdrew** it; **2013 European Public Prosecutor** → Commission pressed on via **enhanced cooperation** (22 states); **2016 posting-of-workers** → Commission found "no case," adopted it (an **East–West split**).

→ A real but limited brake — the lecture's "subnational component."
cards.hint: Yellow = review; orange = kill (never used).

cards.front: Alongside legislation, the EU's **money** runs on its own track *(Bulmer)*. Walk through the **MFF**, the **annual budget**, and **discharge** — and what happens if there's no budget by 1 January.
cards.back:
**MFF (multi-annual financial framework)** — the **~7-year** spending envelope. Proposed by the Commission but **fought out in the European Council and agreed by *unanimity*** — every state has a **veto** on the big number. *(2014–20 MFF ~€960 bn: the UK, backed by NL & Sweden, forced real-terms cuts; **Merkel brokered** it.)*

**Annual budget** — follows an **OLP-like** cycle: Commission drafts, **Council + EP co-decide** (Conciliation Committee if they clash). **No budget by 1 January → "provisional twelfths"** (1/12 of last year's budget per month).

**Discharge** — the **EP formally signs off** that money was spent properly, informed by the **Court of Auditors'** report.

→ Money = where the **intergovernmental** European Council sets the ceiling and the **supranational** EP polices spending.
cards.hint: MFF (unanimity) → annual (OLP-like) → EP discharge.

cards.front: **Adoption ≠ implementation.** Who actually applies EU rules once they're passed? Trace the chain.
cards.back:
The EU **makes** rules but rarely **applies** them itself — **implementation is mostly national** (a defining feature of the EU's "**small state**" design):

**EU organs** adopt the legal framework →
**National administrations** apply the rules in practice →
**National courts / authorities** handle individual cases →
**European Commission** monitors compliance →
**CJEU** settles disputes over EU law.

→ Most EU law is enforced by **national officials**, not Brussels.
cards.hint: EU adopts; member states apply.

cards.front: The EU has **three main legal instruments** that create different degrees of central control. Distinguish **regulation · directive · decision** by binding force and whether national transposition is needed.
cards.back:
**Regulation** — **directly applicable**: becomes law in every state **as written**, automatically. **No transposition** → strongly supranational.
**Directive** — binding as to the **result/objective**, but leaves the **means** to states. **Yes** — states must **transpose** it into national law (choosing *how*) → softer, more flexible.
**Decision** — **binding in full** on **specific addressees** (a state, company or individual). **No transposition** — applies directly to whom it names → a targeted order.

**Different instrument = different degree of central control.**

*(Bulmer:* directives transpose in **two stages** — into law, then application on the ground — and compliance varies. **Recommendations & opinions** exist too but have **no legal force**. Some binding acts are **non-legislative**, e.g. a Commission competition fine.)*
cards.hint: Same-law-everywhere / goal-only / named-target.

cards.front: **Where the EU lacks competence to legislate (e.g. employment, social inclusion), states instead compare best practice and set voluntary targets — no binding law, just peer pressure and learning.** Name this governance mode *(Bulmer)*.
cards.back:
The **Open Method of Coordination (OMC)** — **soft law**.

It sits **beyond the three legal instruments**: no binding regulation/directive/decision, just **benchmarking, best-practice exchange and voluntary targets** where the EU can't legislate. Evidence that "the EU is a very political animal."

*(Related soft instruments with no legal force: **recommendations & opinions**.)*
cards.hint: Soft law by peer pressure, not binding.

cards.front: The EU integrates in **two directions**. Distinguish **positive** from **negative integration** — and which institution drives each.
cards.back:
**Positive integration** — EU institutions **build** common rules: legislation, **harmonization**, common standards. *(Constructing a shared framework — driven by the legislative bodies.)*

**Negative integration** — EU law **removes** national barriers: the **CJEU** interprets the treaties so incompatible national rules **fall away**. *(Clearing obstacles to the four freedoms — driven by the courts.)*

→ One **builds**, the other **clears**; negative integration lets the single market deepen without new legislation (see *Cassis*).
cards.hint: Build common rules vs strike down national barriers.

cards.front: **Germany blocked a French blackcurrant liqueur for being below its minimum alcohol content; the CJEU struck the barrier down (1979) and established that a good lawfully sold in one state may be sold throughout the EU.** Name the case and principle — and which integration theory it exemplifies.
cards.back:
**Cassis de Dijon (1979)** → the principle of **mutual recognition**: a good **lawfully sold in one member state** may in principle be **sold throughout** the EU, even without harmonized rules.

It illustrates **negative integration through courts** — the CJEU removing a national barrier to the **free movement of goods**, deepening the single market **without any new legislation**.

**Theory:** a textbook **neofunctionalist "integration through law"** — courts advancing integration autonomously. *(LI reading: states tolerate it because it serves their collective interest in a working market.)*
cards.hint: Blackcurrant liqueur → mutual recognition.

cards.front: A state breaks EU law. Trace the **infringement route** — who acts, under which articles, and what can happen at the end *(Bulmer)*.
cards.back:
The **Commission**, as **Guardian of the Treaties**, issues a **reasoned opinion** (**Art. 258 TFEU**). If the state still won't comply, it takes it to the **CJEU**.

Since **Maastricht**, the CJEU can impose **financial penalties** (**Art. 260**). Before Maastricht, a losing state faced only **moral pressure**.

Enforcement is **shared**: **Commission** monitors & prosecutes · **national authorities** enforce domestically · **national courts** apply EU law in individual cases (and can refer questions to the CJEU) · **CJEU** gives authoritative interpretation · **Court of Auditors** audits finances.
cards.hint: Reasoned opinion (258) → CJEU → fines (260, since Maastricht).

cards.front: **Why does the architecture matter?** State the two reasons the "typical" model (Commission → EP + Council → law) isn't universal — with the clearest exception.
cards.back:
**① It varies by policy area.** The standard supranational model dominates the **single market** and most regulation, but some areas stay **intergovernmental** — above all the **Common Foreign & Security Policy (CFSP)**: driven by the **European Council + Council**, **unanimity** generally required, and **limited roles** for Commission, EP and CJEU.

**② Membership is differentiated** — not every state joins every policy (euro, Schengen).

→ "The EU" is really **several decision-systems at once**. Where it's more **supranational**, integration can run ahead of states; where **intergovernmental**, states stay in charge. *Same Union, different rules.*
cards.hint: Varies by policy + differentiated membership.

cards.front: How does **CFSP** work — the most intergovernmental corner of the EU *(Bulmer)*? Name the machinery, the **two escape valves**, and the sign that even here integration creeps.
cards.back:
**Machinery:** run by the **European Council** (strategy, by **unanimity**), the **Foreign Affairs Council**, and the **High Representative (HRUFASP)** — **double-hatted** as a **Commission Vice-President** (Ashton → Mogherini → **Borrell**), backed by the EU's diplomatic service, the **EEAS**. Decisions are mostly **declaratory, non-legislative**; the **CJEU is excluded**.

**Two escape valves:** **① "constructive abstention"** — a state can abstain (not block) and isn't bound; **② Art. 31(2) TEU safeguard** — pleading "**vital reasons of national policy**" stops a QMV vote, kicking it to the European Council *(a CFSP-only Luxembourg Compromise)*.

**Yet integration creeps:** the **EEAS** socializes national + EU diplomats, and in **2018 states launched defence cooperation — PESCO** — via enhanced cooperation.
cards.hint: European Council + High Rep + EEAS; abstention & the vital-interest brake.

cards.front: **Differentiated integration:** the EU is common *and* varied. Give the examples for **euro**, **Schengen**, and the rules for **enhanced cooperation** *(Bulmer)*.
cards.back:
**Euro** — **not all** members use the single currency (Denmark opted out; others haven't joined).
**Schengen** — **differentiated**: some EU states out, some **non-EU states in** (Norway, Switzerland).
**Enhanced cooperation** — a **group can move ahead** without the others.

**Enhanced-cooperation rules:** minimum **9 states**, only in **non-exclusive** areas, as a **last resort**, must stay **open** to others; acts **bind only participants** and are **not part of the acquis**. Real uses: the **financial-transaction ("Tobin") tax**, **cross-border divorce law**, the **EU patent** (25 states, minus Italy & Spain), **PESCO** (defence, 2017). Cousin: the **Fiscal Compact** (2012) — a treaty binding **22 states** (UK & Czechia out).

→ How a Union of 27 keeps deepening without lockstep.
cards.hint: Euro & Schengen opt-outs; enhanced cooperation = 9+ move ahead.

cards.front: Name each **Lisbon flexibility valve** *(Bulmer)*: (a) a state fearing an outvote can suspend the procedure and appeal to the European Council; (b) a clause letting the Council switch an area to QMV/OLP **without a new treaty**.
cards.back:
(a) The **emergency brake** — in a few sensitive areas (social security, judicial cooperation, CFSP), a state can **suspend the procedure and appeal to the European Council** — a sovereignty escape hatch.

(b) **Passerelle ("gangway") clauses** — let the Council **switch an area to QMV/OLP without a new treaty** (always *toward* supranationalism). Juncker called them "**lost treasure**" (2018) — but they need **unanimity + EP consent**, and **by 2019 had never been used**.
cards.hint: Pull the brake vs press the (never-used) button.

cards.front: In **1990** the Commission built a **maternity-rights** proposal on a **health-&-safety** treaty article (Art. 118A), and the UK objected to the *base* and threatened the CJEU. Why does the choice of article matter so much — and what general lesson does this teach?
cards.back:
Because power flows from the **treaty base**, *which article a proposal is built on* decides **which procedure and voting rule** apply. Art. 118A triggered **QMV** rather than **unanimity** — so the Commission's choice of base was a move to **strip the UK of its veto** (they settled before the CJEU ruled).

**General lesson:** the **choice of legal base is itself a site of conflict** — pick the article, and you decide **who can block you**. Conflict in the architecture is **structural** — over who initiates, over the money, and over the legal base.
cards.hint: Article → voting rule → who can veto.

cards.front: The **supranational/intergovernmental split IS the LI-vs-neofunctionalism debate.** Fill the grid: for each theory give the **key actors, key mechanism, key EU bodies, and view of integration**.
cards.back:
**Liberal Intergovernmentalism (LI):**
- Key actors: **member-state governments**
- Key mechanism: **interstate bargaining**
- Key bodies: **European Council + Council**
- View: integration stays **under state control**

**Neofunctionalism / Supranationalism:**
- Key actors: **supranational bodies & non-state actors**
- Key mechanism: **spillover**
- Key bodies: **Commission + EP + CJEU**
- View: integration can develop **beyond state control**

→ Whether the **supranational** or the **intergovernmental** bodies dominate a policy area decides whether integration is **state-controlled or self-propelling**.
cards.hint: Governments/bargaining/inter-bodies vs supra-actors/spillover/supra-bodies.

cards.front: The exam move: **read the same institution two ways.** Give the **LI** and **neofunctionalist** reading of each — (a) QMV, (b) the Commission's right of initiative, (c) the CJEU + *Cassis*, (d) CFSP + unanimity.
cards.back:
**(a) QMV** — *LI:* states **agreed** the rules and still bargain (kept unanimity for sensitive stuff); *NF:* accepting you can be **outvoted** is states **losing control**.
**(b) Right of initiative** — *LI:* a convenient agenda-setter serving state-agreed goals; *NF:* the engine of **cultivated spillover**.
**(c) CJEU + Cassis** — *NF:* **integration through law**, courts removing barriers autonomously; *LI:* states tolerate it because it serves their **collective** market interest.
**(d) CFSP + unanimity** — *LI:* proof states keep the **veto** where sovereignty is dearest; *NF:* the **limit** of spillover — an area still "**encapsulated**."

**Template:** name the feature → give the state-control reading → give the beyond-control reading.
cards.hint: Every feature has a state-control and a beyond-control reading.

cards.front: In one arc, state **the heart of the lecture** — the "typical" way an EU law is made, and the red thread that ties the whole architecture together.
cards.back:
EU authority is **pooled, delegated and shared** across **levels** (EU ↔ member state) and across **bodies that each represent a different interest**.

**The typical law:** **Commission proposes → Parliament + Council co-decide** (the **OLP**, usually by **QMV**) **→ member states implement → Commission + CJEU enforce.**

But the model **changes across policy areas** (some stay intergovernmental, e.g. CFSP) and membership is **differentiated** (euro, Schengen).

**Red thread:** the split between **supranational** bodies (Commission · EP · CJEU) and **intergovernmental** bodies (European Council · Council) *is* the institutional form of the **neofunctionalism-vs-LI** debate.
cards.hint: Propose → co-decide → implement → enforce; supra vs inter.

cards.front: Two "apex" nuances that complicate the tidy picture: how has the **European Council** risen, and why is the architecture NOT a Montesquieu separation of powers? *(Bulmer)*
cards.back:
**The European Council has risen to the "apex."** Even though it **cannot legislate**, it now **shapes the context** of nearly everything — agenda, budget ceilings, crisis deals — "**integration without supranationalisation**" (Fabbrini & Puetter). A strongly **intergovernmental** trend.

**Not Montesquieu:** the institutions are a **functional division of labour**, not a separation of powers — the European Council directs, the Commission initiates + guards + implements, Council + EP co-legislate, CJEU + Court of Auditors watchdog. **Powers are shared, not separated** — a **fusion** held together by engineered **cooperation** (IIAs, Conciliation Committees) and pulled apart by **structural conflict** ("institutions matter" — new institutionalism, Keohane).
cards.hint: European Council at the apex; fusion, not separation.
